_meta.provenance: Original questions written for this app. Not copied from AICPA releases or any review course.

questions.stem: Under the FASB Conceptual Framework, which is an ENHANCING (not fundamental) qualitative characteristic?

explain.simple: Two things make information useful at all: it must matter (relevance) and be honest (faithful representation). Other things, like being easy to compare with last year, make good information even better.
steps: Fundamental: relevance and faithful representation.
Enhancing: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability.
Materiality is an entity-specific aspect of relevance.
explain.trap: Memory aid for enhancing: 'CVTU' (Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, Understandability).

questions.stem: Predictive value and confirmatory value are ingredients of which qualitative characteristic?

explain.simple: Information is relevant if it helps you guess the future (predictive) or check whether your past guesses were right (confirmatory).
steps: Relevance = predictive value + confirmatory value (+ materiality).
Faithful representation = complete, neutral, free from error.
explain.trap: Don't put 'neutral' or 'free from error' under relevance. Those belong to faithful representation.

questions.stem: Net income is $100,000. Depreciation is $20,000, accounts receivable increased by $15,000 and accounts payable increased by $5,000. Cash flow from operating activities (indirect method) is:

explain.simple: Start with profit. Add back depreciation (no cash left). Customers owe you more, so cash didn't arrive (subtract). You owe suppliers more, so you kept cash (add).
explain.trap: Asset increases are subtracted and liability increases are added. Reverse the signs for decreases.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, how is interest PAID by a company classified in the statement of cash flows?
options: Either operating or financing, by policy choice

explain.simple: US GAAP treats interest as a normal cost of running the business, like wages, so it goes in operating. Dividends paid are a payment to owners, so they go in financing.
steps: US GAAP: interest paid, interest received and dividends received are operating.
Dividends paid are financing.
IFRS allows a policy choice. US GAAP doesn't.
explain.trap: D is the IFRS (and Ind AS) answer. Read whether the question says US GAAP.

questions.stem: An aging analysis says the allowance for credit losses should be $10,000. Before adjustment, the allowance has a $3,000 credit balance. Credit loss (bad debt) expense for the year is:

explain.simple: You need ₹10,000 in the 'bad debts bucket'. It already holds ₹3,000, so you top it up by ₹7,000. The top-up is the expense.
steps: Required ending allowance = 10,000.
Existing credit balance = 3,000.
explain.trap: If the allowance had a DEBIT balance of 3,000, the expense would be 13,000. Check the side.

questions.stem: Under the CECL model (ASC 326), when are expected credit losses on trade receivables recognised?
options: Only when a loss is probable
Lifetime expected losses, from initial recognition

explain.simple: CECL says: the day you make the sale on credit, estimate how much of it you probably won't collect over its whole life, and record that right away. Don't wait for trouble.
steps: CECL = Current Expected Credit Loss.
Recognise lifetime expected losses at initial recognition.
Use past experience, current conditions and reasonable forecasts.
explain.trap: 'Probable' was the old incurred-loss model. '12-month' is IFRS 9 stage 1.

questions.stem: A FIFO company holds inventory costing $50,000. Its estimated selling price is $52,000 and estimated costs to sell are $7,000. The write-down required is:

explain.simple: Inventory can't stay on the books at more than you'll actually get for it. You'll get 52,000 minus 7,000 selling costs = 45,000. It's on the books at 50,000, so write it down by 5,000.
steps: FIFO/average: lower of cost or NRV.
explain.trap: LIFO and retail-method companies still use lower of cost or MARKET, with a ceiling and floor.

questions.stem: A machine's price is $100,000. Freight in is $2,000 and installation $3,000. Repairs for damage caused by careless handling AFTER delivery are $1,000. The capitalised cost is:

explain.simple: Everything you must spend to get the machine to your factory and working counts as the machine's cost. Fixing damage your own staff caused is a mistake, not part of the cost.
steps: Capitalise price + freight + installation = 105,000.
Expense the 1,000 repair. It wasn't necessary to get the asset ready for use.
explain.trap: Normal testing costs ARE capitalised. Abnormal costs (damage, waste) are not.

questions.stem: Equipment held and used has a carrying amount of $500,000. Undiscounted future cash flows are $450,000 and fair value is $380,000. The impairment loss under US GAAP is:

explain.simple: Step 1: will this machine earn back what it's on the books for, ignoring interest? 450 < 500, so no, and it's impaired. Step 2: write it down to what it could be sold for today (380).
steps: Recoverability test: undiscounted CF 450,000 < CA 500,000, so impaired.
No reversal later under US GAAP for assets held and used.
explain.trap: $50,000 measures the loss against undiscounted cash flows. They are used only to TEST, never to MEASURE.

questions.stem: Under US GAAP, research and development costs (other than those acquired in a business combination or certain software) are:
options: Capitalised once technical feasibility is reached
Deferred until the product is sold

explain.simple: Spending on research is like buying lottery tickets. Nobody knows if it will pay off, so US rules say treat it as a cost today.
steps: ASC 730: R&D is expensed as incurred.
Exceptions: software to be sold (capitalise after technological feasibility), and R&D assets acquired in a business combination.
explain.trap: IFRS/Ind AS 38 capitalises DEVELOPMENT costs once criteria are met. US GAAP doesn't.

questions.stem: For a public business entity, goodwill acquired in a business combination is:
options: Not amortised, but tested for impairment at least annually

explain.simple: Goodwill is the 'extra' paid for a business's reputation and customers. Public companies don't spread it as a cost each year. They check yearly whether it has lost value.
steps: Public entities: no amortisation, annual impairment test at reporting-unit level.
Private companies may elect to amortise over up to 10 years (accounting alternative).
explain.trap: Option A is the PRIVATE company alternative. Check the entity type in the question.

questions.stem: On 1 January, Alpha pays $1,000,000 for 30% of Beta and gains significant influence. Beta earns $200,000 and pays $50,000 in dividends during the year. Alpha's investment balance at 31 December is:

explain.simple: Owning 30% means your 'slice' grows when the company earns profit (your share is 60,000). When the company pays you cash dividends, your slice shrinks, because cash moved out to you (15,000).
steps: Share of income = 30% × 200,000 = 60,000 (increase).
Share of dividends = 30% × 50,000 = 15,000 (decrease).
explain.trap: Under the equity method, dividends are NOT income. They reduce the investment.

questions.stem: Unrealised holding gains on available-for-sale DEBT securities are reported in:

explain.simple: AFS bonds are 'maybe I'll sell, maybe not'. Their paper gains are parked in a side account (OCI) until sold.
steps: Trading debt: fair value through net income.
AFS debt: fair value through OCI.
Held-to-maturity: amortised cost.
Equity securities (no significant influence): fair value through net income.
explain.trap: Since ASU 2016-01 there is no AFS category for EQUITY securities. Their gains go to net income.

questions.stem: Under ASC 842, how does a LESSEE present the expense of an OPERATING lease in the income statement?
options: A single lease cost, generally straight-line
Rent expense only when paid in cash
No expense: only the liability is reduced

explain.simple: Both lease types go on the balance sheet under US rules. But an operating lease shows ONE smooth rent-like cost each year, while a finance lease shows interest plus amortisation, which is higher at the start.
steps: Operating lease: single lease cost, straight-line over the term.
Finance lease: interest on the liability + amortisation of the ROU asset (front-loaded).
explain.trap: Ind AS 116 and IFRS 16 have NO operating lease for lessees. Every lease shows interest + depreciation.

questions.stem: Bonds with face $1,000,000 and a 7% annual coupon have a carrying amount of $950,000. The market rate at issue was 8%. Using the effective interest method, this year's discount amortisation is:

explain.simple: The company really pays 8% on what it borrowed (950,000), which is 76,000. But only 70,000 cash goes out. The 6,000 gap is added to the loan, which creeps up towards 1,000,000.
steps: Interest expense = 950,000 × 8% = 76,000.
Amortisation = 76,000 − 70,000 = 6,000. Carrying amount becomes 956,000.
explain.trap: Expense uses CARRYING amount × MARKET rate. Cash uses FACE × COUPON.

questions.stem: A lawsuit loss is probable. Counsel estimates the range as $200,000–$500,000, with no amount in the range more likely than any other. Under US GAAP the company accrues:

explain.simple: If you'll probably lose and can estimate it, you must record it. If every number in the range is equally likely, US rules say record the lowest one and tell readers the loss could be up to 500,000.
steps: Probable + reasonably estimable means accrue.
No best estimate in the range: accrue the MINIMUM (US GAAP).
Disclose the possible additional loss.
explain.trap: IFRS/Ind AS 37 uses the MIDPOINT (350,000) in this situation.

questions.stem: A company uses accelerated depreciation for tax and straight-line for books. The resulting temporary difference creates a:

explain.simple: Taking bigger tax deductions now means paying less tax today and more tax later. 'Pay later' is a liability.
steps: Tax depreciation > book depreciation now, so taxable income < book income now.
It reverses later, so taxable income will be higher later.
Future taxable amounts mean a deferred tax liability.
explain.trap: Ask 'will I pay MORE tax in future?' Yes = DTL. Will I pay LESS? = DTA.

questions.stem: At year-end, taxable temporary differences are $100,000. The current tax rate is 21%, but a law already ENACTED sets a 25% rate for the years the differences reverse. The deferred tax liability is:

explain.simple: Deferred tax is tax you'll pay in the future, so use the rate that will apply then, as long as the law has actually been passed.
steps: Use the enacted rate for the reversal years: 25%.
explain.trap: Proposed (not enacted) rate changes are ignored under US GAAP. IFRS uses 'substantively enacted'.

questions.stem: Net income is $500,000. Cumulative preferred dividends for the year are $50,000 (not declared). Weighted average common shares are 100,000. Basic EPS is:

explain.simple: EPS is the profit that belongs to ordinary shareholders, per share. Preference shareholders get first claim on 50,000 even if it hasn't been paid yet, because it's cumulative.
explain.trap: Cumulative preferred dividends are deducted whether declared or not. Non-cumulative ones only if declared.

questions.stem: There are 100,000 shares outstanding on 1 January. On 1 July the company issues 20,000 new shares for cash. The weighted average shares for the calendar year is:

explain.simple: The new shares only existed for half the year, so they count as half: 20,000 × 6/12 = 10,000 extra.
explain.trap: Stock dividends and splits are applied RETROACTIVELY to the start of the year. Only real issues are time-weighted.

questions.stem: A SMALL stock dividend (less than 20–25% of outstanding shares) is recorded by transferring from retained earnings an amount equal to the shares'

explain.simple: A small free-share bonus doesn't really change the share price much, so it's treated like giving away shares worth their market price.
steps: Small stock dividend: debit retained earnings at FAIR value.
Large (over 20–25%): usually at PAR value.
Stock split: no entry (memo only).
explain.trap: India's bonus-share accounting differs (usually at face value from reserves). Don't mix it up with US GAAP.

questions.stem: P pays $900,000 for 80% of S. The fair value of the noncontrolling interest is $200,000. The fair value of S's identifiable net assets is $950,000. Goodwill is:

explain.simple: Add up the total value of the whole company (what you paid for your 80% plus what the other 20% is worth). Subtract the fair value of the things you can actually identify. The leftover is goodwill.
steps: Less identifiable net assets 950,000.
Goodwill = 150,000 (full goodwill method under US GAAP).
explain.trap: $140,000 = 900,000 − 80% × 950,000 is the partial-goodwill method. US GAAP requires full goodwill.

questions.stem: In consolidated financial statements, the noncontrolling interest is presented:
options: In equity, separately from the parent's equity

explain.simple: The minority owners are still OWNERS of the group, just not the parent. So they sit in equity, in their own line.
steps: ASC 810: NCI is equity, shown separately.
Consolidated net income is split between parent and NCI.
explain.trap: Redeemable NCI at an SEC registrant may go to mezzanine equity. That's a special case, not the general rule.

questions.stem: A company changes the estimated useful life of equipment from 10 to 8 years. This is accounted for:
options: As a cumulative-effect adjustment in income

explain.simple: New information changed your guess. You don't rewrite the past. You just use the better guess from now on.
steps: Change in estimate: prospective.
Change in principle: retrospective.
Correction of an error: restatement (prior-period adjustment).
explain.trap: A change in depreciation METHOD is a change in estimate effected by a change in principle, so it's also prospective.

questions.stem: A phone (standalone price $600) and a 1-year service plan (standalone price $400) are sold together for $900. How much of the price is allocated to the phone?

explain.simple: The bundle gives a 10% discount. Share the discount fairly in proportion to each item's normal price.
steps: Total standalone prices = 1,000.
Phone share = 600 / 1,000 = 60%.
explain.trap: Allocate the discount to ALL obligations proportionally, unless there's evidence it belongs to only one.

questions.stem: Which situation results in revenue recognised OVER TIME under ASC 606?
options: Customer pays in advance for goods shipped next month
Customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs
The entity retains title until payment
The contract has a return right

explain.simple: Cleaning services: each day the office gets cleaned, the customer gets the benefit that day. So revenue is earned bit by bit, over time.
steps: Over-time criteria (any one): (1) customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit, (2) performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls, (3) no alternative use AND an enforceable right to payment for work done.
Otherwise, recognise at a point in time.
explain.trap: Advance payment creates a contract LIABILITY. It doesn't change when revenue is recognised.

questions.stem: A city's general capital assets (e.g., roads and buildings used by governmental activities) are reported in:
options: Government-wide statement of net position only
Both the General Fund and government-wide statements

explain.simple: The city's monthly budget (General Fund) only tracks spendable money, and you can't spend a road. The big picture (government-wide) shows everything the city owns.
steps: Governmental funds use the current financial resources focus, so no capital assets.
Government-wide statements use the economic resources focus, so capital assets are included and depreciated.
explain.trap: Proprietary funds (e.g., water utility) DO report their capital assets in fund statements.

questions.stem: Under ASU 2016-14, a not-for-profit reports net assets in which classes?
options: With donor restrictions and without donor restrictions

explain.simple: A charity's money is split by one simple question: did the donor put conditions on how it's used?
steps: Two classes: with donor restrictions, and without donor restrictions.
Board designations are WITHOUT donor restrictions (the board can undo them).
explain.trap: Option A is the old three-class model, replaced by ASU 2016-14.

questions.stem: A donor's pledge to a NFP is CONDITIONAL on the NFP raising matching funds (a barrier plus a right of return). The NFP should:
options: Recognise revenue when the condition is substantially met
Recognise revenue when cash is received, regardless of the condition

explain.simple: 'I'll give you ₹1 lakh IF you raise ₹1 lakh yourselves' isn't a gift yet. It becomes one when you hit the target.
steps: Conditional contribution: barrier + right of return/release.
Recognise when the barrier is overcome.
Cash received early is a refundable advance (liability).
explain.trap: Don't confuse conditions (a barrier) with restrictions (a purpose or time limit). Restricted gifts ARE recognised immediately.

questions.stem: Before accepting an audit engagement, the successor auditor should communicate with the predecessor auditor:
options: With the client's permission, about integrity of management, disagreements and reasons for change
Only after the audit report is issued

explain.simple: Before you take a new job, you call the person who had it before to ask 'any problems I should know about?' You need the client's permission to do that.
steps: Ask the client for permission to talk to the predecessor.
Inquire about management integrity, disagreements, fraud or illegal acts, and reasons for the change.
If the client refuses permission, consider the implications for acceptance.
explain.trap: Communication is REQUIRED before acceptance. Reviewing the predecessor's working papers is optional, and happens after acceptance.

questions.stem: Why is performance materiality set LOWER than materiality for the financial statements as a whole?
options: To reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected plus undetected misstatements exceed overall materiality

explain.simple: If your car can carry 500 kg, you plan for 400 kg, leaving room for things you didn't notice you packed. Performance materiality is that safety buffer.
steps: Small misstatements add up.
A lower threshold for testing leaves a cushion for undetected errors.
It is a matter of judgement (often 50–75% of overall materiality in practice).
explain.trap: No standard fixes a percentage. It is judgement.

questions.stem: Analytical procedures are REQUIRED at which stages of an audit?
options: Planning and the overall review near the end
All three: planning, substantive and final review

explain.simple: Auditors must look at the big-picture numbers at the start (to spot risky areas) and at the end (to check everything makes sense). In the middle, it's optional.
steps: Planning (risk assessment): required.
Substantive analytics: optional, a choice of procedure.
Final overall review: required.
explain.trap: 'All three' is the trap. Substantive analytical procedures are a choice, not a requirement.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the five components of internal control under the COSO framework?

explain.simple: COSO describes a company's OWN system for keeping things right. The outside auditor is not part of the company's controls.
steps: COSO components: Control environment, Risk assessment, Control activities, Information & communication, Monitoring.
Memory aid: 'CRIME' (Control env, Risk assessment, Information, Monitoring, Existing control activities).
explain.trap: External audit can never substitute for an entity's internal control.

questions.stem: For good segregation of duties, which functions should be performed by DIFFERENT people?
options: Authorisation, recording, and custody of assets

explain.simple: If one person can approve a payment, hold the cash and write the books, they can steal and hide it. Splitting the jobs means stealing needs two people to cooperate.
steps: Separate: Authorisation, Recordkeeping, Custody (memory aid: 'ARC').
Also separate reconciliation from these duties where possible.
explain.trap: Collusion can defeat segregation of duties. It is an inherent limitation.

questions.stem: Which audit evidence is generally MOST reliable?
options: A bank confirmation received directly by the auditor
A photocopy of a supplier statement provided by the client

explain.simple: Hearing it straight from an outsider, delivered directly to you, beats anything the company tells or hands you.
steps: More reliable: external sources, obtained directly by the auditor, in documentary form, originals, strong controls.
A bank confirmation meets all of these.
explain.trap: Even a CFO's statement is weak evidence on its own. Inquiry alone is never sufficient.

questions.stem: To test the COMPLETENESS assertion for sales, the auditor should select items from:
options: The sales journal and vouch to shipping documents
Shipping documents and trace to the sales journal
The general ledger and vouch to invoices

explain.simple: Completeness asks 'did anything get left OUT of the books?' So start with real-world evidence (what was shipped) and check it made it INTO the books.
steps: Completeness: source document → records (trace).
Existence/occurrence: records → source document (vouch).
explain.trap: Direction is everything. Starting from the journal can never find something that is missing from it.

questions.stem: Confirmation of accounts receivable PRIMARILY provides evidence about which assertion?

explain.simple: Asking the customer 'do you really owe us ₹50,000?' proves the customer and the debt exist. It doesn't prove they'll actually pay.
steps: AR confirmation mainly tests existence (and rights).
Collectability (valuation) is tested via subsequent receipts and the aging.
explain.trap: A customer confirming a balance does not prove they'll pay it.

questions.stem: In substantive sampling, the risk of INCORRECT ACCEPTANCE relates to the audit's:

explain.simple: Accepting a wrong balance as right is the dangerous mistake: the audit failed. Rejecting a right balance just means extra work, so it's merely inefficient.
steps: Incorrect acceptance (Type II / beta risk): effectiveness, the dangerous one.
Incorrect rejection (Type I / alpha risk): efficiency.
For tests of controls: risk of assessing control risk too low = effectiveness.
explain.trap: Memory aid: 'Accept the wrong one and you're IN trouble' (INeffective).

questions.stem: Holding everything else constant, which change INCREASES the required sample size for a substantive test?
options: Increase in the assessed risk of material misstatement
Increase in acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance

explain.simple: The riskier the area, the more items you need to check to be confident.
steps: Sample size goes UP with higher RMM, higher expected misstatement and lower tolerable misstatement.
It goes UP with LOWER acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance.
explain.trap: Tolerable misstatement moves the OPPOSITE way to sample size.

questions.stem: The auditor concludes there is substantial doubt about going concern, and management's disclosure is adequate. The opinion is:
options: Unmodified, with a separate going concern section

explain.simple: If the company honestly tells readers 'we might not survive', the accounts are still fair. The auditor gives a clean opinion but adds a big signpost about the risk.
steps: Adequate disclosure: unmodified opinion + 'Substantial Doubt About the Entity's Ability to Continue as a Going Concern' section.
Inadequate disclosure: qualified or adverse (a misstatement).
explain.trap: A disclaimer is possible only in rare cases of multiple uncertainties. It is not the default.

questions.stem: After year-end but before the report date, a major customer goes bankrupt because of a financial decline that had been happening for several months. This is:
options: A non-recognised subsequent event: disclose only
A recognised subsequent event: adjust receivables
Reported only in next year's statements

explain.simple: The customer was already sick at year-end. The bankruptcy just revealed it. So the year-end receivable was already worth less, and you fix the numbers.
steps: Condition existed at the balance sheet date: recognised (Type 1), so adjust.
Condition arose after year-end (e.g., a fire): non-recognised (Type 2), so disclose if material.
explain.trap: A sudden post-year-end disaster (flood, fire) causing the bankruptcy would be non-recognised.

questions.stem: The management representation letter should be dated:
options: As near as practicable to, but not after, the auditor's report date

explain.simple: Management signs it at the very end, confirming that nothing has changed right up to the day the auditor signs the report.
steps: Representations cover all periods in the report.
Dated as of (no later than) the auditor's report date.
explain.trap: Management representations do NOT replace other audit evidence.

questions.stem: A review engagement under SSARS provides:
options: Limited assurance, mainly via inquiry and analytical procedures

explain.simple: Audit = 'I checked thoroughly' (reasonable assurance). Review = 'I asked questions and looked at trends, nothing looked wrong' (limited). Compilation = 'I just put it together' (none).
steps: Audit: reasonable assurance.
Review (AR-C 90): limited assurance; inquiry + analytics.
Compilation (AR-C 80): no assurance.
explain.trap: A review needs independence. A compilation doesn't, but lack of independence must be disclosed.

questions.stem: In a PCAOB audit report of an issuer, matters that were communicated to the audit committee, relate to material accounts and involved especially challenging judgement are called:

explain.simple: Same idea, two names. US public-company audits say 'critical audit matters'. International and Indian audits say 'key audit matters'.
steps: PCAOB AS 3101: critical audit matters (CAMs).
AICPA AU-C 701 / ISA 701 / SA 701: key audit matters (KAMs).
explain.trap: Read which standard-setter the question mentions: PCAOB means CAM.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who learns that a client made an error on a filed return must:
options: Correct the return without telling the client
Promptly advise the client of the error and its consequences
Report the client to the IRS immediately

explain.simple: Your duty is to tell your client what went wrong and what could happen. Fixing it is the client's decision. You don't secretly fix it, and you don't report them.
steps: §10.21: advise the client promptly of the noncompliance, error or omission and its consequences.
There is no duty to inform the IRS, and you can't correct it without client consent.
explain.trap: Whether to keep working for the client is a separate ethics judgement. It isn't required immediately.

questions.stem: The general statute of limitations for IRS assessment of additional tax is extended to 6 years when the taxpayer:
options: Omits more than 25% of gross income stated on the return

explain.simple: Normally the IRS has 3 years to come back for more tax. Leave out a big chunk of income (over a quarter) and it gets 6 years. Fraud means forever.
steps: General: 3 years from the later of the due date or the filing date.
Over 25% gross income omission: 6 years.
Fraud or no return: unlimited.
explain.trap: Fraud is NOT 6 years. It is unlimited.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old signs a contract to buy a motorbike (not a necessity). The contract is generally:

explain.simple: The law protects young people. A minor can cancel such a deal, but the adult seller can't.
steps: Minors lack full capacity.
The contract is voidable by the MINOR (they may disaffirm during minority or a reasonable time after).
For necessaries, the minor is liable for reasonable value.
explain.trap: Under India's Contract Act, a minor's agreement is VOID ab initio (Mohori Bibee case), which is different from the US rule.

questions.stem: A principal is bound by a contract an agent made without actual authority if the third party reasonably believed, based on the PRINCIPAL's conduct, that the agent had authority. This is:

explain.simple: If the owner lets someone act like the manager for months, customers can rely on that, even if the owner never actually gave permission.
steps: Apparent authority comes from the principal's manifestations to the third party.
The principal is bound to the third party, and may then sue the agent.
explain.trap: The AGENT's own claims can't create apparent authority. It must come from the principal.

questions.stem: A purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in CONSUMER goods is perfected:
options: Only by filing a financing statement

explain.simple: When a store lends you money to buy its TV, its claim on the TV is protected automatically. No paperwork filing is needed.
steps: Attachment = value given + debtor has rights + security agreement.
PMSI in consumer goods: automatically perfected on attachment (except motor vehicles, which need a title notation).
explain.trap: Automatic perfection doesn't beat a good-faith consumer buyer from the consumer unless a filing was made.

questions.stem: Rita exchanges investment land (basis $300,000, FMV $500,000) for other investment land (FMV $450,000) plus $50,000 cash. Her recognised gain and the basis of the new land are:

explain.simple: Swapping land for land isn't taxed. But the cash she pocketed is taxed. The untaxed part of the gain carries into the new land, giving it a lower basis.
steps: Recognised = lesser of boot (50,000) or realised gain = 50,000.
explain.trap: Since 2018, §1031 applies ONLY to real property.

questions.stem: Generally, the basis of property INHERITED from a decedent is:
options: Fair market value at the date of death (or alternate valuation date if elected)
The lower of the decedent's basis or FMV

explain.simple: When you inherit, the tax 'price tag' resets to what the thing was worth when the person died. The growth during their life escapes income tax.
steps: §1014: stepped-up (or down) basis to FMV at death.
Alternate valuation date: 6 months later, if the executor elects it.
explain.trap: Gifts take the donor's basis. Inheritances get FMV. Check which one the question describes.

questions.stem: A partner contributes $50,000 cash. Her share of partnership income is $20,000, she receives $10,000 in distributions, and her share of partnership liabilities increases by $5,000. Her ending outside basis is:

explain.simple: Her 'investment meter' goes up with money put in, profits earned and her share of the firm's debts. It goes down with cash she takes out.
steps: Increase in share of liabilities = deemed cash contribution.
explain.trap: Basis can't go below zero. Distributions above basis trigger gain.

questions.stem: Which would PREVENT a corporation from electing S corporation status?
options: Having voting and non-voting common stock

explain.simple: S corps are a special US tax shortcut for small, mostly-local owner groups. A foreign (non-resident) owner breaks the rules.
steps: Requirements: domestic corporation, ≤100 shareholders, ONE class of stock, eligible shareholders (individuals, certain trusts and estates; no nonresident aliens, no corporations or partnerships).
Differences only in voting rights don't create a second class.
explain.trap: Voting vs non-voting common is allowed. Different economic rights (distributions) would be a second class.

questions.stem: A C corporation owns 30% of another domestic corporation. Its dividends-received deduction percentage is generally:

explain.simple: To stop the same profit being taxed again and again as it passes between companies, a company gets a deduction on dividends from other companies. The more it owns, the bigger the deduction.
steps: Under 20% ownership: 50%.
80% or more (affiliated group): 100%.
Subject to taxable-income limits.
explain.trap: These percentages apply post-2017 (TCJA). Older books show 70% and 80%.

questions.stem: To qualify for long-term capital gain treatment, a capital asset generally must be held for:

explain.simple: Hold an investment for over a year and the US taxes the profit at lower, long-term rates.
steps: Long-term: held MORE than 1 year.
Gifted property usually tacks on the donor's holding period.
Inherited property is always long-term.
explain.trap: India's holding periods differ by asset. Don't mix the two regimes.

questions.stem: Net §1231 GAINS for the year (after the 5-year look-back for prior §1231 losses) are treated as:

explain.simple: Business property sold at a profit gets the nice capital-gain rate. Sold at a loss, you get a full ordinary deduction. Best of both worlds.
steps: Net §1231 gain: LTCG (after recapturing net §1231 losses deducted in the prior 5 years as ordinary).
Net §1231 loss: ordinary loss.
Depreciation recapture (§1245/§1250) is taken out first.
explain.trap: Don't forget the look-back rule. It converts part of the gain to ordinary income.

questions.stem: Which bankruptcy chapter is primarily a LIQUIDATION of the debtor's non-exempt assets?

explain.simple: Chapter 7: sell everything and pay creditors what you can. Chapter 11: the business keeps running while it restructures its debts. Chapter 13: an individual repayment plan.
steps: 7 = liquidation.
11 = reorganisation (mainly businesses).
13 = individual debt adjustment.
9 = municipalities.
explain.trap: Chapter 11 may also be used by individuals with large debts.

questions.stem: A taxpayer transfers land (basis $40,000, FMV $100,000) to a new corporation solely for stock, and is in control (80% or more) immediately after. The basis of the stock received is:

explain.simple: Starting a company with your own land isn't a sale, so no tax now. The untaxed gain hides in the shares by keeping the old basis.
steps: §351 applies, so no gain is recognised.
Stock basis = property basis 40,000 (+ gain recognised − boot − liabilities assumed).
The corporation's basis in the land is also 40,000 (carryover).
explain.trap: Services contributed for stock are NOT property under §351. They are taxable compensation.

questions.stem: Cost of goods sold is $600,000 and average inventory is $150,000. Inventory turnover and days in inventory (365-day year) are approximately:

explain.simple: The shop empties and refills its shelves 4 times a year, so each batch sits about 3 months (91 days).
explain.trap: Use COGS, not sales, for inventory turnover. Use sales for receivables turnover.

questions.stem: Net profit margin is 5%, asset turnover is 2.0 and the equity multiplier (assets/equity) is 1.5. Return on equity is:

explain.simple: ROE has three levers: how much profit per sale, how many sales per rupee of assets, and how much borrowed money boosts it.
steps: DuPont: ROE = margin × turnover × leverage
explain.trap: Higher leverage raises ROE but also risk. Examiners ask what DRIVES an ROE change.

questions.stem: When production EXCEEDS sales, operating income under absorption costing compared with variable costing is:

explain.simple: Absorption costing tucks part of the factory's fixed cost into unsold stock on the shelf. That cost isn't expensed yet, so profit looks higher.
steps: Absorption: fixed manufacturing overhead is inventoried.
Production > sales means some fixed overhead is deferred in ending inventory.
Difference = change in inventory units × fixed overhead per unit.
explain.trap: When sales exceed production the reverse is true: absorption income is lower.

questions.stem: Actual labour hours are 1,100. Standard hours allowed for actual output are 1,000. Standard rate is $20/hour and actual rate $21/hour. The labour EFFICIENCY variance is:

explain.simple: Workers took 100 hours more than they should have. Each hour is valued at the PLANNED rate of $20, so 2,000 wasted.
steps: Rate variance (separate) = (AR − SR) × AH = 1 × 1,100 = 1,100 U
explain.trap: Efficiency variances use the STANDARD rate. Rate variances use ACTUAL hours.

questions.stem: A part can be bought for $22. Making it costs $18 variable plus $6 of allocated fixed overhead that will continue either way. On cost alone, the company should:

explain.simple: The $6 rent-type cost is paid whether you make it or not, so ignore it. Compare only what changes: $18 to make vs $22 to buy.
steps: Relevant cost to make = avoidable cost = 18.
Buy = 22.
Make saves 22 − 18 = 4 per unit.
explain.trap: Allocated, unavoidable fixed costs (and sunk costs) are irrelevant. Consider qualitative factors and opportunity cost of capacity too.

questions.stem: In a qualifying CASH FLOW hedge, changes in the fair value of the hedging derivative included in the assessment of effectiveness are initially recorded in:
options: Other comprehensive income, then reclassified to earnings when the hedged item affects earnings
As an adjustment to the hedged item's carrying amount

explain.simple: A cash flow hedge protects a FUTURE payment. The hedge's gains and losses are parked in OCI and released into profit exactly when the future payment hits profit, so the two cancel out.
steps: Cash flow hedge: OCI, then reclassified when the forecast transaction affects earnings.
Fair value hedge: both derivative and hedged item go through earnings (basis adjustment).
explain.trap: Option D describes a FAIR VALUE hedge.

questions.stem: Which cost is IRRELEVANT when deciding whether to replace an old machine?
options: Purchase price of the new machine
Book value of the old machine
Salvage value of the old machine today
Operating costs saved by the new machine

explain.simple: What you paid for the old machine years ago is gone whatever you do now. Only future money that differs between the choices matters.
steps: The book value of the old asset is a sunk cost, so it's irrelevant.
Relevant: new cost, today's disposal value, operating savings, tax effects.
explain.trap: The TAX effect of a loss on disposal IS relevant, even though book value itself is sunk.

questions.stem: Which is an APPLICATION control rather than an IT general control?
options: Restricting access to the data centre
Edit check rejecting invoices with a missing vendor ID

explain.simple: General controls protect the whole IT environment (locks, change rules, backups). Application controls live inside one program and check each transaction, like a form that won't accept a blank field.
steps: ITGCs: access, program changes, program development, computer operations.
Application controls: input, processing and output controls within a system (e.g., validity, completeness and limit checks).
explain.trap: Weak ITGCs undermine reliance on ALL application controls.

questions.stem: Which change-management weakness is MOST significant?
options: Developers can move their own code into production without independent approval
Testing is done in a separate test environment
Users sign off on test results

explain.simple: If the person writing the code can also switch it on in the live system, they could slip in anything, including a fraud.
steps: Key control: segregate development from production migration.
Approval + testing + independent migration.
explain.trap: Options C and D are GOOD controls, included to distract you.

questions.stem: To create a digital signature that proves a message came from Sender A, the message hash is encrypted with:

explain.simple: Only A has A's private key, like a personal seal. Anyone can check the seal with A's public key, which proves it really was A.
steps: Signature: sign with the SENDER's private key, verify with the sender's public key.
Confidentiality: encrypt with the RECIPIENT's public key, decrypt with the recipient's private key.
explain.trap: Swap the keys and you get confidentiality, not authentication.

questions.stem: A recovery point objective (RPO) of 4 hours means:
options: Systems must be back online within 4 hours
The business can tolerate losing up to 4 hours of data
Users get 4 hours' notice of an outage

explain.simple: RPO = how far BACK in time you can afford to lose work. RTO = how fast you must be running AGAIN.
steps: RPO is about data loss (it drives backup frequency).
RTO is about downtime (it drives recovery capability).
explain.trap: Option A describes RTO.

questions.stem: A SOC 1 report lists 'complementary user entity controls' (CUECs). These are:
options: Controls the service auditor tested at the user entity
Controls the USER entity must have for the service organisation's control objectives to be achieved

explain.simple: The payroll provider's controls work only if YOU do your part, like sending the correct employee list. Those 'your part' controls are CUECs.
steps: CUECs are assumed in the design of the service organisation's controls.
The user auditor must test CUECs at the user entity.
explain.trap: Subservice-organisation controls are 'CSOCs', a different concept.

questions.stem: Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of account takeover after a successful phishing attack captures a password?

explain.simple: Even if a thief has your password, they still need the code sent to your phone. That's multi-factor authentication.
steps: MFA is something you know + have + are.
Training is preventive but weaker once credentials have already been stolen.
explain.trap: Frequent forced password changes are NOT recommended by modern guidance (NIST).

questions.stem: A married couple elects GIFT SPLITTING. The effect on gifts to each child is that:
options: Each gift is treated as made one-half by each spouse, doubling the annual exclusion available per donee
The unified credit is doubled for life
Gift tax returns are no longer required

explain.simple: Even if only one spouse writes the cheque, the couple can treat it as half from each, so each child can receive twice the tax-free annual amount.
steps: §2513 election: both spouses consent.
Each spouse can use their own annual exclusion per donee.
A gift tax return (Form 709) is still required to make the election.
explain.trap: Gifts are never income-tax deductible for the donor (unless to charity).

questions.stem: Life insurance on the decedent's life is included in the gross estate if:
options: Never: life insurance is always excluded
The decedent held incidents of ownership, or the proceeds are payable to the estate
Only if the beneficiary is a child
Only if the policy was bought in the last 3 years

explain.simple: If the person who died still controlled the policy (could change beneficiaries, borrow against it), the payout counts as part of what they owned.
steps: §2042: included if payable to the estate OR the decedent had incidents of ownership.
Transfers of ownership within 3 years of death are pulled back in (§2035).
explain.trap: An irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) is used to keep proceeds OUT of the estate.

questions.stem: Land with basis $60,000 is sold for $100,000 under an installment sale. $30,000 is collected in year 1. Gain recognised in year 1 is:

explain.simple: 40% of the price is profit. So each rupee you collect is 40% profit. Collect 30,000, and you've realised 12,000 of profit.
explain.trap: Depreciation recapture must be recognised in the year of sale, regardless of payments.

questions.stem: The main tax disadvantage of a C corporation compared with a partnership or S corporation is:
options: Double taxation of earnings distributed as dividends

explain.simple: The company pays tax on its profit. When it pays you a dividend from what's left, you pay tax again on the same money.
steps: C corp: entity-level tax + shareholder dividend tax.
Partnerships and S corps are flow-through, taxed once at owner level.
explain.trap: Limited liability is an ADVANTAGE of corporations, not a disadvantage.

questions.stem: Qualified distributions from a Roth IRA are:
options: Taxable only on the earnings portion

explain.simple: With a Roth you pay tax on the money going in. If you follow the rules, everything coming out later, including growth, is tax-free.
steps: Contributions are after-tax.
Qualified distribution: 5-year rule + age 59½, death, disability, or first-home (limited).
Then fully tax-free.
explain.trap: Non-qualified distributions of EARNINGS can be taxed and penalised. Contributions come out first, tax-free.
